In bellwether Minais Gerais, with polls about even, president’s supporters are striving to win over those who abstained or voted for Flavio Bolsonaro

Naiara Boroni, Nikolas Domingues and Jodersson Diego live in the same city and do not know one another, but said they had done the same thing in recent days: persuaded at least one person who had not voted for the leftist president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in the first round to choose him in this Sunday’s runoff.

In Boroni’s case, it was her grandmother who had not turned out; in Domingues’s, a cousin who had chosen a candidate who finished fourth. But Diego achieved what to many sounds almost impossible in such a polarised country: he said he had persuaded a woman who voted for the far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro to switch sides.

articles.title: Blockades, checkpoints and court action: fending off Brazil’s biofuel giants in the Amazon
articles.summary:
After decades of violent displacement and land theft, the country’s quilombola communities are fighting back

For most of his 39 years, Josias Dias dos Santos, known as Jota, has endured degrading cycles of displacement as a quilombola, a descendant of Black people once enslaved on Brazil’s sugar cane and coffee plantations. He says his and other quilombola families subsisting in the rainforests in Pará, northern Brazil, were first forced out of their settlements by violent loggers, then by ranchers and miners.

Yet, they say the worst came with the arrival of the palm oil industry in what is now the country’s most deforested state. Palm oil companies producing biofuels and supplying global customers, subsidised by the federal government, have laid claim to ever larger tracts of traditional quilombola territory over the past two decades.

Jorge Luis Zambrano, alias “Rasquiña” or “JL,” was the charismatic leader of the Choneros, which, for years, was Ecuador’s most enterprising and powerful criminal group. Rasquiña oversaw the group’s transformation from a localized criminal group into a nationwide prison-based criminal federation with links to transnational drug-trafficking organizations. He was assassinated in 2020.

Meanwhile, Colombia and Mexico face escalating political friction and security crises linked to organized crime and controversial law enforcement actions. The security landscape is further complicated by severe infrastructure damage from storms in Brazil and persistent drug-related violence and cartel activity in Ecuador and Colombia.

archive.forecast_en: Over the coming days, all attention will focus on the results of the Brazilian presidential runoff, which will determine the political and economic trajectory of Latin America's largest economy. The region is simultaneously grappling with macroeconomic pressures from global markets, including Brent oil rising to $109/bbl, alongside heightened geopolitical cooperation between the US and Argentina targeting organized crime.

archive.forecast_en: In the coming hours, all attention will focus on the results of the Brazilian presidential run-off, which will determine the country's future direction and Amazon rainforest protections. Commodity markets will continue to reflect oil price dynamics and record coffee valuations.

archive.forecast_en: In the coming hours, all attention will focus on the results of the Brazilian presidential runoff, which will determine the country's future political trajectory. Commodity markets will continue to reflect record coffee prices and global energy instability.

Region nadále čelí externím tlakům spojeným s kolísáním globálních cen komodit, rostoucím napětím na Blízkém východě a přetrvávajícími bezpečnostními riziky spojenými s organizovaným zločinem v Andském regionu a na Haiti.
